entries.caption: Albert I (1875–1934), King of the Belgians and commander of the Belgian army, who refused the German ultimatum and held Liège, Antwerp and finally the Yser. Photographed in 1917 in the post-1915 khaki uniform and Adrian helmet. Colorized (AI-assisted) from a public-domain photograph.
entries.credit: Original photograph: Richard Neville Speaight, 1917, The World's Work 1919; public domain (via Wikimedia Commons). Colorization: Sandtable, AI-assisted, 2026.
entries.licence: public domain — author died 1938; published before 1931

entries.caption: Otto von Bismarck in 1890 — the year Wilhelm II dismissed him and let his treaty with Russia lapse. Colorized (AI-assisted) from a public-domain photograph.
entries.credit: Original photograph: Jacques Pilartz, Cologne, 1890; Internet Archive Book Images via Wikimedia Commons; public domain. Colorization: Sandtable, AI-assisted, 2026.
entries.licence: public domain — no known copyright restrictions (Internet Archive Book Images); the photographer died in 1910

entries.caption: Karl von Bülow (1846–1921), commander of the German 2nd Army — Liège, Namur, Charleroi, Guise; his call for Kluck to wheel inward and his decision to retreat from the Marne on 9 September, in consultation with Hentsch. Photographed c. 1916 as Generalfeldmarschall. Colorized (AI-assisted) from a public-domain photograph.
entries.credit: Original photograph: Rudolf Dührkoop, c. 1916, Berliner Illustrirte Zeitung; public domain (via Wikimedia Commons). Colorization: Sandtable, AI-assisted, 2026.
entries.licence: public domain — photographer died 1918 (life + 70); published before 1931

entries.caption: Édouard de Castelnau (1851–1944), commander of the French 2nd Army — attacked into Lorraine under Plan XVII, was thrown back at Morhange, then held the Grand Couronné before Nancy while the Marne was fought; he lost three sons in the war. Colorized (AI-assisted) from a public-domain photograph.
entries.credit: Original photograph: unknown, c. 1915; public domain (via Wikimedia Commons). Colorization: Sandtable, AI-assisted, 2026.
entries.licence: public domain / CC0 per Commons; weak provenance chain — find the underlying Gallica/Agence Rol print for the pipeline

entries.caption: Winston Churchill (1874–1965), First Lord of the Admiralty 1911–1915 — sent the Royal Naval Division to Antwerp in October 1914 and went there himself; a cross-era figure who reappears at Gallipoli, in the interwar years and in 1940. Colorized (AI-assisted) from a public-domain photograph.
entries.credit: Original photograph: agency stringer, 16 Sept 1914; public domain (via Wikimedia Commons). Colorization: Sandtable, AI-assisted, 2026.
entries.licence: public domain in the United States (published before 1931); confirm status outside the US

entries.caption: Erich von Falkenhayn (1861–1922), Prussian Minister of War from 1913 and, from 14 September 1914, Moltke's successor as Chief of the General Staff — the man who took the war to the Race to the Sea and Ypres. Colorized (AI-assisted) from a public-domain photograph by Albert Meyer, c. 1913–14.
entries.credit: Original photograph: Albert Meyer, Berlin, c. 1913–14; public domain (via Wikimedia Commons; Bundesarchiv Bild 146-2004-0023). Colorization: Sandtable, AI-assisted, 2026.
entries.licence: public domain (photographer died 1924; life + 100 years)

entries.caption: Ferdinand Foch (1851–1929), commander of the new 9th Army at the Marne — held the marshes of Saint-Gond against Bülow and Hausen ('my centre is giving way, my right is retreating; situation excellent, I attack'); Supreme Allied Commander in 1918. Colorized (AI-assisted) from a public-domain photograph; the horizon-blue uniform post-dates 1914.
entries.credit: Original photograph: Sport & General, Nationaal Archief 158-1095, CC0 (via Wikimedia Commons). Colorization: Sandtable, AI-assisted, 2026.
entries.licence: CC0 1.0 (Nationaal Archief public-domain dedication)

entries.caption: Louis Franchet d'Espèrey (1856–1942), 'Desperate Frankie' to the British — led I Corps at Guise, replaced Lanrezac at the head of the 5th Army on 3 September, and drove into the gap beside the BEF at the Marne; commanded the Salonika breakthrough in 1918. Colorized (AI-assisted) from a public-domain photograph; the horizon-blue uniform post-dates 1914.
entries.credit: Original photograph: Henri Manuel, BnF Gallica; public domain (via Wikimedia Commons). Colorization: Sandtable, AI-assisted, 2026.
entries.licence: public domain — photographer died 1947 (life + 70)

entries.caption: Field Marshal Sir John French (1852–1925), Commander-in-Chief of the British Expeditionary Force 1914–1915 — Mons, Le Cateau, the retreat, and a reluctant return to the line at the Marne. Colorized (AI-assisted) from a public-domain photograph; uniform colour interpretive.
entries.credit: Original photograph: Hainer, Paris, period postcard; public domain (via Wikimedia Commons). Colorization: Sandtable, AI-assisted, 2026.
entries.licence: public domain — published before 1 January 1931

entries.caption: Joseph Gallieni (1849–1916), Military Governor of Paris from 26 August 1914 — read the aviators' reports of Kluck's turn and threw the 6th Army at the exposed German flank; the taxis were his. Colorized (AI-assisted) from a public-domain photograph.
entries.credit: Original photograph: Bain News Service, 1910, Library of Congress; public domain (via Wikimedia Commons). Colorization: Sandtable, AI-assisted, 2026.
entries.licence: public domain — LoC: no known copyright restrictions; pre-1931; PD Mark 1.0

entries.caption: Sir Douglas Haig in September 1914, when he commanded I Corps of the British Expeditionary Force — in reserve at Mons, then the retreat, the Marne and the Aisne. Colorized (AI-assisted) from a public-domain press photograph.
entries.credit: Original photograph: Agence Rol, September 1914; Bibliothèque nationale de France, EST EI-13 (391), Rol 42304, via Gallica; public domain. Colorization: Sandtable, AI-assisted, 2026.
entries.licence: public domain in France and the United States — an Agence Rol press photograph of 1914; the agency's work is out of copyright

entries.caption: Max von Hausen (1846–1922), commander of the Saxon 3rd Army — Dinant and the Meuse crossing, the Sambre with Bülow, and the night assault on Foch at the marshes of Saint-Gond; relieved, ill with typhus, after the Marne. Colorized (AI-assisted) from a public-domain photograph (c. 1900, in full dress).
entries.credit: Original photograph: Otto Mayer, Dresden, c. 1900, Bildarchiv Austria; public domain (via Wikimedia Commons). Colorization: Sandtable, AI-assisted, 2026.
entries.licence: public domain — life + 70 (photographer) / published before 1931

entries.caption: Richard Hentsch (1869–1918), Oberstleutnant of the General Staff — sent by Moltke on 8 September 1914 to tour the army headquarters with authority to order a retreat; his visit to Bülow and Kluck on 8–9 September ended the German advance at the Marne. Photographed in 1918. Colorized (AI-assisted).
entries.credit: Original photograph: J. F. R. von Goetz, 1918, Deutsche Digitale Bibliothek, CC-BY 3.0 (via Wikimedia Commons). Colorization: Sandtable, AI-assisted, 2026.
entries.licence: CC-BY 3.0 DE (attribution: Landesarchiv Baden-Württemberg, HStA Stuttgart M 703 R959N4) and public domain in the US (pre-1931)

entries.caption: Joseph Joffre (1852–1931), Commander-in-Chief of the French armies 1914–1916 — author of Plan XVII and of the retreat and counterstroke that won the Marne. Colorized (AI-assisted) from a public-domain photograph.
entries.credit: Original photograph: BnF Gallica, photographer unknown; public domain (via Wikimedia Commons). Colorization: Sandtable, AI-assisted, 2026.
entries.licence: public domain (France; pre-1931)

entries.caption: Alexander von Kluck (1846–1934), commander of the German 1st Army — the outer edge of the wheel, who fought the BEF at Mons and Le Cateau and turned southeast short of Paris, opening the gap the Allies struck at the Marne. Colorized (AI-assisted) from a public-domain photograph.
entries.credit: Original photograph: Mayer, Dresden; postcard by Gustav Liersch & Co., Berlin, c. 1914; public domain (via Wikimedia Commons, Wartenberg Trust). Colorization: Sandtable, AI-assisted, 2026.
entries.licence: public domain — published before 1 January 1931 (United States)

entries.caption: Charles Lanrezac (1852–1925), commander of the French 5th Army — saw the German wheel coming before Joffre believed it, was mauled at Charleroi, counterattacked at Guise, and was dismissed on 3 September, three days before the Marne. Colorized (AI-assisted) from a public-domain photograph.
entries.credit: Original photograph: anonymous, reproduced in Hanotaux, Histoire illustrée de la guerre de 1914 (1916); public domain (via Wikimedia Commons). Colorization: Sandtable, AI-assisted, 2026.
entries.licence: public domain — anonymous work, copyright expired (US and EU)

entries.caption: Gérard Leman (1851–1920), commander of the fortified position of Liège — held the ring of forts from 4 August until he was pulled unconscious from the ruins of Fort Loncin on 15 August; the delay cost the German timetable its first days. Colorized (AI-assisted) from a public-domain photograph (1918, after his release from captivity).
entries.credit: Original photograph: anonymous, 1918; public domain (via Wikimedia Commons). Colorization: Sandtable, AI-assisted, 2026.
entries.licence: public domain — anonymous work published before 1931

entries.caption: Erich Ludendorff (1865–1937) — as a staff officer at Liège on 7 August 1914 he drove to the citadel and took its surrender, then went east to Tannenberg as Hindenburg's chief of staff; by 1916 he ran the German war effort. Photographed in 1915. Colorized (AI-assisted).
entries.credit: Original photograph: Bundesarchiv, Bild 183-2005-0828-525 / CC-BY-SA 3.0. Colorization: Sandtable, AI-assisted, 2026, CC-BY-SA 3.0 DE.
entries.licence: CC-BY-SA 3.0 DE — required attribution: "Bundesarchiv, Bild 183-2005-0828-525 / CC-BY-SA 3.0" (the photograph may also be PD by age, but we honour the Bundesarchiv terms)

entries.caption: Michel-Joseph Maunoury (1847–1923), recalled from retirement to command the new 6th Army — struck Kluck's exposed flank on the Ourcq on 5–6 September 1914, the blow that opened the Marne; blinded by a bullet in 1915. Colorized (AI-assisted) from a public-domain photograph.
entries.credit: Original photograph: Bain News Service, Library of Congress; public domain (via Wikimedia Commons). Colorization: Sandtable, AI-assisted, 2026.
entries.licence: public domain — published before 1931 (LoC Bain: no known restrictions)

entries.caption: Helmuth von Moltke the Elder (1800–1891), Chief of the Prussian General Staff, photographed by Carl Günther in the 1870s. Colorized (AI-assisted) from a public-domain photograph.
entries.credit: Original photograph: Carl Günther, 1870s; Bibliothèque nationale de France (Gallica), via Wikimedia Commons; public domain. Colorization: Sandtable, AI-assisted, 2026.
entries.licence: public domain — photographer died 1905, photograph taken in the 1870s; Commons: public domain

entries.caption: Helmuth von Moltke the Elder in the full dress of a Generalfeldmarschall, about 1889 — eighty-nine years old, a year from retirement's end and two from his death, wearing the orders of the three wars that made Germany. Colorized (AI-assisted) from a public-domain photograph.
entries.credit: Original photograph: photographer not identified, c. 1889; via Wikimedia Commons; public domain. Colorization: Sandtable, AI-assisted, 2026.
entries.licence: public domain — PD-old-70-expired and PD Mark 1.0 per Commons; published well before 1931

entries.caption: Helmuth von Moltke the Younger (1848–1916), Chief of the General Staff 1906–1914, who inherited Schlieffen's plan and altered it. Photographed in 1906 on taking office. Colorized (AI-assisted) from a public-domain photograph.
entries.credit: Original photograph: E. Bieber studio, 1906, published in Die Woche; public domain (via Wikimedia Commons). Colorization: Sandtable, AI-assisted, 2026.
entries.licence: public domain — published before 1 January 1931; Commons Public Domain Mark 1.0

entries.caption: Rupprecht, Crown Prince of Bavaria (1869–1955), commander of the German 6th Army — the hinge at Metz; his counteroffensive in Lorraine (20 Aug) and assault on the Grand Couronné drew the left wing into battle Schlieffen meant it to avoid. Colorized (AI-assisted) from a public-domain photograph.
entries.credit: Original photograph: Bernhard Dittmar, c. 1914, Library of Congress; public domain (via Wikimedia Commons). Colorization: Sandtable, AI-assisted, 2026.
entries.licence: public domain — photographer died 1939; published before 1931

entries.caption: Alfred Graf von Schlieffen (1833–1913), Chief of the German General Staff 1891–1906, author of the December 1905 memorandum. Colorized (AI-assisted) from a public-domain photograph.
entries.credit: Original photograph: public domain (archive to confirm). Colorization: Sandtable, AI-assisted, 2026.
entries.licence: public domain — published before 1 January 1931 (Commons: PD in the United States; note the rule-of-the-shorter-term caveat outside the US)

entries.caption: Wilhelm II in the white full dress of the Garde du Corps, photographed by the court photographers Reichard & Lindner in 1905 and sold as a postcard — the Kaiser as he wished to be seen. Colorized (AI-assisted) from a public-domain photograph.
entries.credit: Original photograph: Reichard & Lindner, Berlin, 1905; published by Gustav Liersch & Co; Deutsches Historisches Museum via Wikimedia Commons; public domain. Colorization: Sandtable, AI-assisted, 2026.
entries.licence: public domain — PD-old, published 1905

entries.caption: Wilhelm II (left) in Russian uniform and his cousin Nicholas II in Prussian uniform, 1905 — the two emperors wearing each other's armies for the camera, nine years before those armies met. Colorized (AI-assisted) from a Bundesarchiv photograph.
entries.credit: Original photograph: Bundesarchiv, Bild 183-R43302 / CC-BY-SA 3.0 (Allgemeiner Deutscher Nachrichtendienst — Zentralbild), 1905. Colorization: Sandtable, AI-assisted, 2026, under the same CC-BY-SA 3.0 licence.
entries.licence: CC-BY-SA 3.0 DE — the attribution string 'Bundesarchiv, Bild 183-R43302 / CC-BY-SA 3.0' is mandatory, and the colorization inherits share-alike

entries.caption: Franz Ferdinand, Sophie and their three children at home in 1910. Their marriage was morganatic and their children barred from the throne; it was their fourteenth wedding anniversary that took them to Sarajevo on 28 June 1914. Colorized (AI-assisted) from a public-domain photograph.
entries.credit: Original photograph: Bain News Service, 1910; Library of Congress, George Grantham Bain Collection (LCCN 2014697443, ggbain.17181); no known restrictions on publication. Colorization: Sandtable, AI-assisted, 2026.
entries.licence: public domain — Library of Congress: no known restrictions on publication; pre-1931

entries.caption: 'Excursion to Paris — see you on the Boulevard.' German infantry in a goods wagon of the Alsace-Lorraine railways, August 1914: the mobilization timetable in human form, and the confidence that it would all be over in six weeks. Colorized (AI-assisted) from a public-domain photograph.
entries.credit: Original photograph: anonymous, August 1914, via greatwar.nl and Wikimedia Commons; public domain. Colorization: Sandtable, AI-assisted, 2026.
entries.licence: public domain — anonymous work, more than 70 years since creation (EU) and published before 1931 (US)

entries.caption: A German 42cm siege howitzer and its crew, the type that broke the Liège and Namur forts in August 1914 — a gun that had to be brought up in pieces and bedded before it could fire. Colorized (AI-assisted) from a public-domain photograph.
entries.credit: Original photograph: photographer not identified, First World War; via Flickr (Alfredo Grados Rivero), marked public domain. Colorization: Sandtable, AI-assisted, 2026.
entries.licence: public domain — the underlying photograph is a German press or army photograph of the First World War, published well before 1931; the Flickr copy is marked public domain

entries.caption: German infantry resting in a snow-filled trench on the Eastern Front, winter 1914–15 — greatcoats, covered Pickelhauben, and one man still watching the parapet. Colorized (AI-assisted) from a public-domain photograph.
entries.credit: Original photograph: photographer not identified, German army, winter 1914–15; public domain. Colorization: Sandtable, AI-assisted, 2026.
entries.licence: public domain — a German photograph of the First World War, published well before 1931

entries.caption: French infantry charging with the bayonet at the Grandes manœuvres of 1913 — the army of Plan XVII a year before it attacked into Lorraine and the Ardennes in the same coats and képis. A peacetime exercise, often miscaptioned as the Marne. Colorized (AI-assisted) from an Agence Rol photograph.
entries.credit: Original photograph: Agence Rol, 1913; Bibliothèque nationale de France, Gallica (btv1b6931787b), via Wikimedia Commons; public domain. Colorization: Sandtable, AI-assisted, 2026.
entries.licence: public domain (agency photograph, France, pre-1931; BnF Gallica)

entries.caption: German soldiers in a motor car on a square in Liège, August 1914, rifles across the folded hood. The city was in German hands from 7 August while the twelve forts around it held out for another nine days. Colorized (AI-assisted) from a public-domain photograph.
entries.credit: Original photograph: photographer not established; published in 'The Great War in Images and Pictures' (Moscow, 1914); public domain. Colorization: Sandtable, AI-assisted, 2026.
entries.licence: public domain — published in the Russian Empire before 7 November 1917, and in the United States before 1 January 1931

entries.caption: Belgian infantry in the fighting line in the suburbs of Herstal, north-east of Liège, August 1914 — the dark blue greatcoat and oilcloth shako the army still wore in 1914. Colorized (AI-assisted) from a public-domain photograph.
entries.credit: Original photograph: photographer not established; published in Le Miroir no. 38 (1914) and in 'The Great War in Images and Pictures' (Moscow, 1914); public domain. Colorization: Sandtable, AI-assisted, 2026.
entries.licence: public domain — published in the Russian Empire before 7 November 1917, and in the United States before 1 January 1931

entries.caption: German infantry in the long grass, rifles levelled, Pickelhauben under their grey covers — captioned as the Marne, September 1914, and possibly posed for the camera: two of the men already wear the Iron Cross. Colorized (AI-assisted) from a public-domain photograph.
entries.credit: Original photograph: German Army, September 1914 (as captioned), via greatwar.nl and Wikimedia Commons; public domain. Colorization: Sandtable, AI-assisted, 2026.
entries.licence: public domain — published before 1931 (US), anonymous work more than 70 years old (EU)

entries.caption: A Company, 4th Battalion, Royal Fusiliers resting in the Grand-Place at Mons on 22 August 1914 — the day before the battle. On the 23rd the battalion held the canal bridge at Nimy and won the first two Victoria Crosses of the war. Colorized (AI-assisted) from a public-domain photograph.
entries.credit: Original photograph: photographer not identified, Mons, 22 August 1914; Imperial War Museums Q 70071; public domain. Colorization: Sandtable, AI-assisted, 2026.
entries.licence: public domain — a work of the United Kingdom government created before 1 June 1957 (PD-UKGov); the photograph dates from 1914

entries.caption: Sophie and Franz Ferdinand in the back of the car at Sarajevo, 28 June 1914 — the last hour of both their lives, and the first link in the chain that followed. Colorized (AI-assisted) from a public-domain photograph.
entries.credit: Original photograph: photographer not identified, Sarajevo, 28 June 1914; Imperial War Museums Q 91848, via Wikimedia Commons; public domain. Colorization: Sandtable, AI-assisted, 2026.
entries.licence: public domain — PD-UKGov for the IWM copy (UK Government work created before 1 June 1957); the photograph itself dates from 1914 and is out of copyright in its country of origin

entries.caption: Franz Ferdinand and Sophie in the open car at Sarajevo on 28 June 1914, the hood folded down and the route lined — minutes from the corner where Princip was standing. Colorized (AI-assisted) from a public-domain photograph.
entries.credit: Original photograph: photographer not identified, Sarajevo, 28 June 1914; Imperial War Museums Q 91848, via Wikimedia Commons; public domain. Colorization: Sandtable, AI-assisted, 2026.
entries.licence: public domain — PD-UKGov for the IWM copy (UK Government work created before 1 June 1957); the photograph itself dates from 1914 and is out of copyright in its country of origin

entries.caption: Haupt, von Oven and von Brandis of the 24th Brandenburg Infantry, the officers credited with taking Fort Douaumont on 25 February 1916 — though it was Haupt's company, and Pionier-Sergeant Kunze who climbed in first; Brandis wrote the book and got the fame. Colorized (AI-assisted) from a public-domain photograph.
entries.credit: Original photograph: Die Woche 1918 Nr. 2, August Scherl Verlag; public domain (via Wikimedia Commons). Colorization: Sandtable, AI-assisted, 2026.
entries.licence: public domain — life + 70 / published before 1931

entries.caption: A ration party of the Royal Irish Rifles in a communication trench on the Somme, July 1916 — one of the most reproduced photographs of the war, and one of the few in which the men look back at you. Colorized (AI-assisted) from a public-domain photograph.
entries.credit: Original photograph: Royal Engineers No 1 Printing Company, July 1916; Imperial War Museums Q 1, via Wikimedia Commons; public domain (PD-UKGov). Colorization: Sandtable, AI-assisted, 2026.
entries.licence: public domain — PD-UKGov, UK Government work created before 1 June 1957

entries.caption: Australian gunners on a duckboard track through what had been Chateau Wood, near Hooge in the Ypres salient, 29 October 1917. The wood is the ground itself, drowned. Colorized (AI-assisted) from a public-domain photograph.
entries.credit: Original photograph: Frank Hurley, 29 October 1917; Australian War Memorial E01220; public domain. Colorization: Sandtable, AI-assisted, 2026.
entries.licence: public domain — Australian official photograph of the First World War, well out of copyright; the AWM makes the image available for public use

entries.caption: One of Liège's own guns, three years on: a Krupp 21 cm turret howitzer from the Belgian forts, converted by the Germans into a field piece and captured at Flesquières by the 1/7th Gordon Highlanders, 24 November 1917. A 1917 photograph (IWM Q 7823), not a Liège one — shown here for what the forts' fall gave the German artillery. Colorized (AI-assisted).
entries.credit: Original photograph: John Warwick Brooke, 24 November 1917, Imperial War Museums Q 7823, via Wikimedia Commons; public domain. Colorization: Sandtable, AI-assisted, 2026.
entries.licence: public domain — UK Crown copyright expired (photograph taken before 1 June 1957); IWM Q 7823
